title: Schneider Electric to Buy PTC for $22.6 Billion in Its Biggest Deal Ever
excerpt: The $205-a-share all-cash offer, a 42.3% premium, sent PTC shares up nearly 34% on Monday. Schneider's stock fell about 10% in Paris as investors weighed the price and the up-to-EUR-23-billion financing plan.
body:
• Schneider Electric agreed on October 5 to buy US industrial software company PTC for $205 a share in cash — valuing equity at $22.6 billion with an enterprise value of $23.7 billion — its largest acquisition ever. Closing is expected in the third quarter of 2027.
  • PTC shares surged nearly 34% on the news; Schneider's shares fell about 10% in Paris trading as investors weighed the size and price of the deal, wiping roughly €15 billion off its market capitalisation.
  • The offer is a 42.3% premium to PTC's October 2 closing price. Schneider plans to fund the deal with up to €17 billion in new debt and up to €6 billion in new equity, and targets €250 million in annual cost synergies plus €800 million in revenue synergies by the third year after closing.
  • Boston-based PTC employs about 7,000 people and serves roughly 30,000 customers, with nearly half its revenue from the Americas. Jefferies said AI disruption fears are letting Schneider buy PTC "at a decade-low valuation."

Schneider Electric struck its biggest deal ever on Monday, agreeing to acquire US industrial software company PTC for $22.6 billion in cash. The French energy and engineering group will pay $205 per PTC share, a 42.3% premium to the October 2 closing price, implying an enterprise value of $23.7 billion. PTC's board has approved the offer; closing is expected in the third quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. PTC shares jumped 34.4% in US premarket trading on the announcement.

Context and Background

The deal deepens Schneider's shift from electrical hardware into software. Once known for fuses and circuit breakers, the company now supplies the backbone of data centres — cooling units, server racks and power distribution equipment — and booming US data-centre demand is driving its earnings. In July it lifted its annual revenue forecast after record first-half results: revenue of €21.2 billion, up 9.8%, and net income of €2.49 billion, up 30%.

It is Schneider's second big software move of the year after agreeing in June to buy Cognite Holding, a provider of AI software and industrial data. PTC — which specialises in computer-aided design software and product-lifecycle-management tools for manufacturing — brings about 7,000 employees, roughly 30,000 customers and an installed base spanning design studios and factory floors.

Impact and Analysis

PTC shareholders got a takeover premium that Jefferies called a decade-low valuation for software assets, as AI advances raise fears of cheaper competing services. Berenberg analyst Nay Soe Naing told Reuters the deal was "a healthy valuation amid a compressed valuation environment and challenging investor sentiment across the software space."

"AI disruption fears are still weighing on software valuations, which allows acquiring PTC at a decade-low valuation."

— Jefferies, in a research note

Schneider shareholders were less enthusiastic. The stock fell nearly 10% in early Paris trading on the size of the acquisition, the premium and the financing — up to €17 billion ($19 billion) in new debt plus up to €6 billion in new shares — wiping close to €15 billion ($17 billion) from Schneider's market capitalisation, even though the stock had been up 29% year-to-date through Friday.

Schneider says the combination "creates a leading, scaled, open and interoperable industrial software and AI franchise." CEO Olivier Blum told investors that PTC's engineering and design data would strengthen Schneider's ability to deploy AI across customers' industrial operations: "Data is becoming a very critical layer" for extracting value from AI. PTC chief executive Neil Barua said the deal gives PTC "substantial scale and resources to accelerate innovation" and reach more geographies and end markets.

Diaspora Angle

The direct impact for Indian readers is limited, but the direction matters: this is another major bet on data-centre and industrial-AI infrastructure, a sector employing a large Indian tech workforce in the US and Europe. Schneider's pivot — from hardware to software-plus-AI — mirrors the skills shift playing out across engineering and enterprise IT hiring globally.

What's Next

Three milestones decide whether this pays off: regulatory clearances across jurisdictions, financing execution — raising up to €23 billion without denting Schneider's credit profile is the central shareholder concern — and delivery on the synergy targets by 2030, against a software market still repricing itself around AI disruption.
